Understanding the ASX 200

The S&P/ASX 200 is Australia's headline share market index. It tracks the 200 largest companies listed on the Australian Securities Exchange, measured by float-adjusted market capitalisation. Standard & Poor's reviews the index quarterly, adding companies that have grown large enough and removing those that have shrunk or been acquired. Because it captures roughly 80 per cent of the total value of the Australian market, the ASX 200 is widely used as the benchmark against which fund managers, index funds and individual investors measure their own performance over any given year.

How the ASX 200 is calculated

The index is market-capitalisation weighted, which means larger companies move the index more than smaller ones. A company's weight is its float-adjusted market value divided by the combined value of all 200 constituents. Float adjustment excludes shares that are closely held and not available for public trading, so a company with a large founder stake carries less weight than its headline market value alone would suggest. As of early 2024, the four major banks and the two largest mining companies together accounted for well over a third of the entire index, which is why movements in those handful of names can dominate a day's trading.

The index is calculated and published in real time during trading hours, which run from 10:00am to 4:00pm Sydney time on business days. The opening and closing levels each day are the figures most commonly quoted in the financial press. Total-return versions of the index also exist, which assume dividends are reinvested; these are a fairer measure of what a long-term investor actually earns, because Australian shares have historically paid relatively high dividends compared with other developed markets.

ASX 200 versus the All Ordinaries

Investors often confuse the ASX 200 with the All Ordinaries index. The All Ordinaries contains roughly 500 companies and is the older of the two, dating back to 1980. The ASX 200 was introduced in 2000 specifically to give institutional investors a cleaner, more liquid benchmark that is easier to replicate with an index fund. In practice the two indices move almost in lock-step, because the additional 300 companies in the All Ordinaries are small and collectively account for only a few per cent of total market value. For most practical purposes the ASX 200 is the number that matters.

How to invest in the ASX 200

The simplest way for an ordinary investor to gain exposure to the ASX 200 is through a low-cost exchange-traded fund that tracks the index. Several providers offer such funds on the exchange, typically charging an annual management fee of less than 0.1 per cent. Buying one unit gives an investor a slice of all 200 companies in a single trade, with dividends usually paid quarterly. This diversification is the main appeal: rather than trying to pick individual winners, an index investor simply owns the whole market and accepts its average return, which over the long run has been in the high single digits including dividends.
